lessons.title: The Three Cash Flows: Operating, Investing and Financing Activities

children.text: Two companies both ended the year with ₹5 crore more in the bank. The first earned it from customers. The second borrowed it from a bank. The bank balance looks identical and the businesses are nothing alike.
The cash flow statement exists to tell those two apart. It splits every rupee that moved into three buckets, and the pattern across those buckets is one of the fastest reads in financial statements.

body.text: The total change in cash tells you almost nothing. Where the cash came from tells you everything.

children.text: The Three Buckets
Ind AS 7 requires every cash flow to fall into one of three activities, in this order.

cells: Cash from running the business day to day
Collections from customers, payments to suppliers and employees, tax paid, working capital movements
Does the core business generate cash?
Cash spent on or received from long-term assets
Buying plant and equipment, buying or selling investments, acquiring a business, interest and dividends received
Is the company building capacity or selling it off?
Cash exchanged with lenders and owners
Loans raised and repaid, interest paid, dividends paid, share issues, buybacks, lease payments
Who is funding the company, and what is it returning to them?

body.text: Read the sections as a hierarchy. Operating cash is earned, investing cash is usually spent by choice, and financing cash is borrowed or returned. A company covering its investing needs out of operating cash is self-funding. One covering them out of financing is dependent on somebody else continuing to say yes.

body.title: Sort the transaction
body.question: Kesari Foods repays ₹80 lakh of principal on its term loan and ₹15 lakh of interest on the same day. Where do these two amounts appear?
options: Principal in financing, interest in operating or financing depending on the company's chosen policy
Principal in investing, interest in operating
body.explanation: Loan principal is always financing. Interest paid is a policy choice for non-financial companies under Ind AS 7: many Indian companies show it under financing, some under operating. Check which one a company uses before comparing its operating cash with a peer.

children.text: The closing figure of ₹1.5 crore is not a new number. It is exactly the cash and cash equivalents line on the balance sheet from Lesson 3.1. The cash flow statement is the explanation of how last year's cash balance became this year's.

body.label: Free cash flow
body.context: Kesari Foods generated ₹2.7 crore from operations and spent ₹3.5 crore on equipment, so free cash flow was negative ₹0.8 crore. The shortfall was funded by borrowing. One year of this while building capacity is normal. Five years of it means the business has never paid for its own growth.

body.title: Calculate free cash flow
body.prompt: A Vadodara chemicals company reports net cash from operating activities of ₹46 crore and spends ₹19 crore on plant and machinery during the year. What is its free cash flow, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹46 crore minus ₹19 crore = ₹27 crore. This is the cash genuinely available to repay debt, pay dividends or fund acquisitions, after keeping the existing asset base running and growing.

children.text: Reading the Pattern of Signs
Before reading any individual number, look at whether each of the three sections is positive or negative. The combination alone identifies what kind of company you are looking at.

cells: A mature, self-funding company. It earns cash, invests some, and returns the rest to lenders and shareholders.
A growing company. Operations generate cash, but expansion needs more, so it raises debt or equity as well.
An early-stage or loss-making company burning cash, funded entirely by investors or lenders. Normal for a startup, alarming for a 30-year-old manufacturer.
Often a company selling assets or investments to repay debt. Sometimes prudent consolidation, sometimes distress.
A serious warning. The business is losing cash and selling assets to pay lenders.

children.text: Infosys in FY25 is the textbook first pattern. On a consolidated basis it generated ₹35,694 crore from operations, used ₹1,864 crore in investing and returned ₹24,161 crore through financing, mostly dividends and buybacks. Cash rose, and it rose because customers paid, not because a bank did.

body.explanation: The purchase is a cash outflow under investing in the year it is paid for. The P&L sees it only later, spread across years as depreciation.

Growth is being paid for by the business itself

Financing: plus ₹13 crore of fresh borrowing

body.text: A single year of negative operating cash proves nothing on its own, and even strong companies have one. What matters is the run: three consecutive years of negative operating cash funded by rising borrowings is the shape almost every Indian corporate collapse took before it became news.

children.text: The Traps in Each Section
Operating:

a company can flatter this figure by delaying supplier payments right before year end. Payables jump, operating cash looks strong, and the payment simply moves into April. Compare payable days across years to catch it.
Investing:

capital expenditure is shown when paid, not when committed. A company can defer payments on a completed plant and show low capex in a year it actually built a lot. The capital commitments note discloses what is contracted but not yet spent.
Financing:
watch the gross figures, not the net. Borrowings raised of ₹50 crore and repaid of ₹48 crore net to ₹2 crore, which hides how much short-term debt is being rolled over continuously.
Across all three:

non-cash transactions never appear here at all. A plant acquired entirely on deferred credit, or a lease signed under Ind AS 116, changes the balance sheet without touching this statement in the year it happens.
Ind AS 7 allows two ways to present operating cash flows.
Indirect method:
start from profit before tax, add back non-cash charges, adjust for working capital. Nearly every Indian company uses this, because it is built from figures the accounts already contain.
Direct method:

list actual cash received from customers and paid to suppliers and employees. It is far easier for a non-finance reader to follow, and it is rare in practice because it needs the underlying cash data to be captured separately.

Both methods give exactly the same operating cash figure. If you ever get to influence how your company presents its internal management accounts, the direct method makes cash conversations dramatically easier with non-finance teams.

body.label: screener.in cash flow tables
body.description: Scroll to the Cash Flows section on any company page to see ten years of operating, investing and financing cash side by side. The sign pattern across a decade is visible in one glance.

body.title: Reading a supplier's cash flow statement
body.scenario: You head procurement at a Gurugram appliances company. A key component supplier wants a three-year exclusive contract and better payment terms. Their P&L looks fine: revenue up 22%, profit up 15%. Their cash flow statement for the last three years reads: operating cash of minus ₹4 crore, minus ₹9 crore and minus ₹14 crore. Investing is negative each year. Financing is positive each year, and borrowings have tripled.
body.prompt: What does this pattern tell you, and what would you do before signing?
body.modelAnswer:
What the pattern says:
1. Growing revenue and profit alongside worsening operating cash means the growth is not being collected. Either receivables are ballooning, or inventory is, or the profit itself is soft.
2. Three years of it is a run, not a blip, and the deterioration is accelerating.
3. Expansion funded entirely by rising borrowings while operations consume cash means lenders are funding both the growth and the losses in cash terms. That works until one lender declines to renew a limit.
4. For me as a customer, the risk is supply failure, not their profit. A supplier that cannot pay its own vendors stops receiving raw material, and my line stops.
What I would do before signing:
5. Ask for their receivable days, inventory days and payable days for the three years, and check whether payables are being stretched to fund the gap.
6. Check their credit rating and any rating rationale from CRISIL, ICRA or CARE Ratings, and look at the auditor's report for going concern language or qualifications.
7. Check MCA filings for charges created on their assets, which shows how much is already pledged.
8. Ask directly what the additional borrowing funded and when operating cash is expected to turn.
What I would propose:
9. Not exclusivity. Dual-source the component, even at a slightly higher landed cost, because the premium is cheaper than a line stoppage.
10. Better terms only against security: shorter payment terms tied to on-time delivery, or advance payments against a bank guarantee.
11. A quarterly review of their financials written into the contract, with an exit right if operating cash does not improve.

body.title: Read one cash flow statement end to end
steps: Open the cash flow statement of your employer or a listed company for the last three years.
Write down the sign of each of the three sections for each year and identify the pattern.
Compute free cash flow for each year: operating cash minus capital expenditure.
Check whether the closing cash figure matches the balance sheet cash line. It must.
Look at gross borrowings raised and repaid under financing, not just the net figure.
Check whether interest paid is shown under operating or financing before comparing with any peer.

cards.definition: Cash from the core business, including working capital movements and tax paid.
Cash spent on or received from long-term assets and investments.
Cash exchanged with lenders and owners: borrowings, interest, dividends, share issues and lease repayments.
Operating cash minus capital expenditure. What is genuinely left over after keeping the business running.
Presenting operating cash by starting from profit and adjusting for non-cash items and working capital.
Presenting operating cash as actual receipts from customers and payments to suppliers and employees.
Contracted capital expenditure not yet paid for, disclosed in the notes rather than in this statement.

points: Every cash movement falls into operating, investing or financing, and the split matters more than the total.
The closing cash in this statement must equal the cash line on the balance sheet.
Free cash flow is operating cash minus capital expenditure. It shows whether a company funds its own growth.
The pattern of signs identifies the company: positive, negative, negative is mature and self-funding, while negative, negative, positive is burning cash on someone else's money.
Interest paid can sit under operating or financing, so check the policy before comparing two companies.
Year-end payable stretching, deferred capex payments and netted borrowings all distort the picture, so read three years together.

body.text: Kesari Foods, the Vadodara chemicals company and the Gurugram appliances supplier are fictional, with figures constructed for teaching. Infosys numbers are FY25 consolidated figures from screener.in. Nothing here is investment advice.
